% =====================================================================
\begin{abstract}
\noindent
The index of substitution saturation $\Iss=\Hbar/\HFSS$
\citep{xia2003iss} is used to decide, before any tree is built, whether an
alignment retains phylogenetic signal. We show that the entropy construction
enters $\E[\Iss]$ only through the spectrum of the rate matrix. On the
eigenbasis of the symmetrised generator the index becomes a linear functional
of the coordinates $\langle e^{\mu d}\rangle$, singling out when it collapses
onto mean pairwise $p$-distance: the ratio of each non-zero eigenvalue's
algebraic multiplicity to its composition weight must be constant across
distinct eigenvalues. It
holds for every reversible model at uniform composition, and for every
composition when the spectrum is degenerate; it fails for non-uniform
composition with a non-degenerate spectrum, the regime it was calibrated in.
Wherever it holds, the index reads nothing about the number of
substitutions realised that the uncorrected proportion of differing sites
does not already supply. The mean of $\lambda$, the other tree-free
index in use, reduces the same way.

The critical value fails separately. It carries no
rate-heterogeneity coordinate, and in the near-saturated region the index is
pinned within a few percent of its upper bound: a two-hundred-fold change in
the tree length needed to make the topology unrecoverable moves it by less
than one percent, so it cannot distinguish moderate from severe saturation. A four-taxon transfer of long branches at fixed patristic total
makes the consequence direct --- the index is constant along the path while
recovery spans its full range.

Real data occupy both regimes: on the data set that introduced the
index the saturated codon partition falls between two readings of its own
threshold; a genome-scale avian alignment, an order of magnitude below both.
Passing the test is evidence against saturation, failing it is weak evidence,
neither is evidence of resolution.
\end{abstract}

% =====================================================================
\section{Introduction}

The index of substitution saturation, $\Iss=\Hbar/\HFSS$, was introduced by
\citet{xia2003iss} to answer a question that substitution models address only
implicitly: have a set of sequences accumulated so many multiple substitutions
that their phylogenetic signal is exhausted? Its construction is deliberately
minimal. $\Hbar$ is the mean entropy of the base composition at a site,
$\HFSS$ the entropy expected under full saturation, so the ratio requires only
an alignment --- no tree, no model fit, no likelihood. That independence is why
it is used: $\Iss$ can be computed before any phylogeny is built, and compared
against a tabulated critical value $\Issc$ to decide in advance whether a data
set is fit for analysis \citep{xia2003iss,xia2009handbook}.

The two halves of the test are constructed differently, and the difference
matters. The index itself is a statistic of the alignment; the critical value
is a threshold calibrated by simulation under specified conditions
\citep{xia2003iss}. Here we characterise the first exactly, and show that the
second fails for reasons that have nothing to do with that characterisation.

We show that the entropy construction enters $\E[\Iss]$ only through the
spectrum of the rate matrix, which reduces the question of what $\Iss$ measures
to a spectral one. Resolving the transition matrix on the eigenbasis of the
symmetrised generator $S=\Pi^{1/2}Q\Pi^{-1/2}$ makes the index a linear
functional of the coordinates $\xi_\mu=\langle e^{\mu d}\rangle$, and singles
out the condition under which it collapses onto mean pairwise $p$-distance:
the ratio $\tau_\mu/w_\mu$ must be constant across the distinct non-zero
eigenvalues of $Q$. The condition is met for every reversible model under
uniform base frequencies and for every composition when the spectrum is
degenerate, and it fails --- mildly, by a term we quantify --- in the
regime used to calibrate $\Iss$. Where it holds, $\Iss$ and mean
$p$-distance induce the same ordering of alignments, so the content of the
test is carried entirely by the critical value. That value we show to be
$L$-dependent, so that the test statistic grows as $\sqrt{L}$, and in the
near-saturated region to be pinned close enough to the index's upper bound
that it cannot track the divergence it is meant to threshold.

% =====================================================================
\section{Results}

\subsection{The statistic and its normalisation}
\label{sec:setting}

Let $N$ sequences of length $L$ be related by a tree $\mathcal{T}$ with leaf
states generated by a reversible rate matrix $Q$ stationary with respect to
$\bpi$, normalised so that $-\sum_j\pi_jQ_{jj}=1$. Write
$\hat{\mathbf p}^{(i)}$ for the empirical state frequencies at site $i$,
$\hat p_j$ for their average over sites (the pooled frequencies), and
\begin{equation}
  H_i=h(\hat{\mathbf p}^{(i)}),\qquad h(\mathbf p)=-\sum_j p_j\ln p_j,\qquad
  \Hbar=\frac1L\sum_{i=1}^{L}H_i .
\end{equation}
The normalising constant admits two readings, and both are needed below:
\begin{equation}
  \HFSS^{(A)}=\E_{\mathbf n\sim\Mult(N,\hat{\mathbf p})}\bigl[h(\mathbf n/N)\bigr],
  \qquad \HFSS^{(B)}=h(\hat{\mathbf p}),
  \label{eq:conventions}
\end{equation}
convention $(A)$ being Xia's \citep{xia2003iss,xia2009handbook} and convention
$(B)$ the plug-in composition entropy. Since
$\HFSS^{(A)}=h(\hat{\mathbf p})-\frac{K-1}{2N}+O(N^{-2})$, the two are related
on any data set by
\begin{equation}
  \Iss^{(A)}=c\,\Iss^{(B)},\qquad
  c=\frac{h(\hat{\mathbf p})}{\HFSS^{(A)}},\qquad c\in(1,\,1.08]\ \text{for }N\ge16 .
  \label{eq:convention}
\end{equation}
Because $c$ depends on $\hat{\mathbf p}$ and not on the tree, it is a constant
within any one alignment: the convention rescales the index but does not
change whether the affine relation holds
(Section~\ref{sec:criterion}), nor which of two alignments is more saturated
when they share a composition. Across data sets with different base
frequencies $c$ differs, so the two conventions need not even agree on the
ordering; the ratio moves by at most $8\%$ over the nucleotide range for
$N\ge16$, but by $51\%$ at $N=4$, where $c=1/0.6620$.

\subsection{Spectral resolution}

Throughout, $\Pi=\operatorname{diag}(\bpi)$ and
\begin{equation}
  S=\Pi^{1/2}Q\,\Pi^{-1/2}=U\Lambda U^{\!\top},\qquad
  \Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_K),\quad
  0=\lambda_1>\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_K .
\end{equation}
Because $Q$ is reversible, $S$ is symmetric, so its eigenvectors are
orthonormal and the spectral projectors are orthogonal:
\begin{equation}
  P_\mu=\sum_{k:\lambda_k=\mu}u_ku_k^{\!\top},\qquad
  \tau_\mu=\tr P_\mu\in\{1,\dots,K-1\},\qquad
  w_\mu=\tr(\Pi P_\mu)=\sum_j\pi_j(P_\mu)_{jj}.
  \label{eq:projectors}
\end{equation}
\begin{lemma}[Spectral resolution]
\label{lem:spectral}
$Q=\Pi^{-1/2}U\Lambda U^{\!\top}\Pi^{1/2}$ and $P(t)=e^{Qt}$, hence
\begin{equation}
  P_{ij}(t)=\pi_j+\sum_{k\ge2}A^{(k)}_{ij}e^{\lambda_kt},\qquad
  A^{(k)}_{ij}=\pi_i^{-1/2}u_{ki}u_{kj}\pi_j^{1/2},\qquad
  A^{(k)}_{jj}=u_{kj}^2 .
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$P(t)=\Pi^{-1/2}Ue^{\Lambda t}U^{\!\top}\Pi^{1/2}$ gives the entries directly.
For $k=1$, $\lambda_1=0$ and $\mathbf u_1=\sqrt{\bpi}$ --- indeed
$S\sqrt{\bpi}=\Pi^{1/2}Q\mathbf 1=\mathbf 0$ --- so
$A^{(1)}_{ij}=\pi_i^{-1/2}\sqrt{\pi_i}\sqrt{\pi_j}\,\pi_j^{1/2}=\pi_j$.
\end{proof}

Because $S$ is symmetric its eigenvectors are orthonormal, so
$\tau_k=\sum_ju_{kj}^2=1$ for every $k$: the grouped coefficient
$\tau_\mu$ in Eq.~\eqref{eq:projectors} \emph{is} the algebraic multiplicity,
with no separate argument needed. In particular
$\tr P(t)-1=\sum_{\mu\ne0}\tau_\mu e^{\mu t}$, so the phylogenetic term
$\Psi=\langle\tr P\rangle-1$ weights each eigenvalue by how many times it
occurs. This is the reason the criterion below is a statement about
\emph{multiplicities} rather than about individual eigenvalues.

\begin{lemma}[The three scalars]
\label{lem:scalars}
With $\langle\cdot\rangle$ averaging over ordered leaf pairs and rate classes,
and $\xi_\mu=\langle e^{\mu d}\rangle$,
\begin{equation}
  \Psi=\sum_{\mu\ne0}\tau_\mu\,\xi_\mu,\qquad
  \wp=\Bigl(1-\sum_j\pi_j^2\Bigr)-\sum_{\mu\ne0}w_\mu\,\xi_\mu,\qquad
  \Delta=\sum_{\mu\ne0}\Bigl(w_\mu-\tfrac{\tau_\mu}{K}\Bigr)\xi_\mu ,
  \label{eq:scalars}
\end{equation}
where $\wp$ is the mean pairwise $p$-distance and
$\Delta=\sum_j(\pi_j-1/K)(\langle P_{jj}\rangle-\pi_j)$ is the
composition-leakage term of Theorem~\ref{thm:affine}.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:spectral},
$\langle P_{jj}\rangle=\pi_j+\sum_{\mu\ne0}(P_\mu)_{jj}\xi_\mu$. Summing over
$j$ gives $\Psi=\sum_j\langle P_{jj}\rangle-1=\sum_{\mu\ne0}\tau_\mu\xi_\mu$;
weighting by $\pi_j$ gives
$\sum_j\pi_j\langle P_{jj}\rangle=\sum_j\pi_j^2+\sum_{\mu\ne0}w_\mu\xi_\mu$,
and $1$ minus that is $\wp$. Finally
$\langle P_{jj}\rangle-\pi_j=\sum_{\mu\ne0}(P_\mu)_{jj}\xi_\mu$, so
$\Delta=\sum_{\mu\ne0}\bigl(w_\mu-\tau_\mu/K\bigr)\xi_\mu$ on substituting
$\sum_j(P_\mu)_{jj}=\tau_\mu$ and $\sum_j\pi_j(P_\mu)_{jj}=w_\mu$.
\end{proof}

Everything the index can see about the tree enters through the single vector
$\bxi$; what distinguishes the three scalars is only how the spectrum is
weighted --- unweighted for $\Psi$, composition-weighted for $\wp$ and
$\Delta$. Section~\ref{sec:criterion} shows that the index collapses onto
$\wp$ exactly when those two weightings agree up to scale.

\subsection{Exact and second-order closed forms}

The index has two closed forms, one asymptotic and one exact on star trees.

\begin{lemma}[Entropy expansion]
\label{lem:entropy}
For $\hat{\mathbf p}$ with $\E[\hat{\mathbf p}]=\bpi$, lying in a compact
neighbourhood of $\bpi$ bounded away from the simplex boundary,
\begin{equation}
  \E\bigl[h(\hat{\mathbf p})\bigr]
  =h(\bpi)-\frac12\sum_j\frac{\Var(\hat p_j)}{\pi_j}+R_3,
  \qquad
  |R_3|\le\frac16\sum_j\frac{\E\bigl[|\hat p_j-\pi_j|^3\bigr]}{\min(\pi_j,\hat p_j)^2}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$\partial h/\partial p_j=-(\ln p_j+1)$, $\partial^2h/\partial p_j^2=-1/p_j$,
$\partial^3h/\partial p_j^3=1/p_j^2$, and the mixed partials vanish. Taylor
expansion at $\bpi$ with Lagrange remainder; the linear term vanishes because
$\E[\hat p_j]=\pi_j$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Variance aggregation]
\label{lem:varagg}
$\Var(\hat p_j)=\dfrac{\pi_j(1-\pi_j)}{N}+\dfrac{N-1}{N}\pi_j
\bigl(\langle P_{jj}\rangle-\pi_j\bigr)$, hence
$\displaystyle\sum_j\frac{\Var(\hat p_j)}{\pi_j}
=\frac{K-1}{N}+\frac{N-1}{N}\Psi .$
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$\Pr(X_i=j,X_{i'}=j)=\pi_jP_{jj}(d_{ii'})$ for leaves $i\ne i'$ by
reversibility and Chapman--Kolmogorov. Summing the $N(N-1)$ ordered
covariances $\pi_jP_{jj}(d_{ii'})-\pi_j^2$ and dividing by $N^2$ gives the
first display; dividing by $\pi_j$ and summing gives
$\sum_j(1-\pi_j)/N=(K-1)/N$ and
$\frac{N-1}{N}\sum_j(\langle P_{jj}\rangle-\pi_j)=\frac{N-1}{N}\Psi$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Second-order closed form]
\label{thm:secondorder}
Under the assumptions above,
\begin{equation}
  \E[\Iss]=1-\frac{1}{2h(\bpi)}\biggl[\frac{K-1}{N}
  +\frac{N-1}{N}\,\bigl\langle\tr P(rd)-1\bigr\rangle\biggr]+O(3).
  \label{eq:secondorder}
\end{equation}
Under JC69 in particular,
$\E[\Iss]=1-\frac{1}{2\ln4}\bigl[\frac3N+\frac{N-1}{N}\,3\,\E_r e^{-8rd/3}\bigr]+O(3)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Sites are independent, so $\E[\Hbar]=\E[h(\hat{\mathbf p})]$ for one site.
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:entropy} and substitute Lemma~\ref{lem:varagg}; divide by
$\HFSS$. For JC69, $h(\bpi)=\ln4$ and $\Psi=3\E_r e^{-8rd/3}$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:spectral} with $t=2rd$.
\end{proof}

The remainder $R_3$ vanishes as some $n_j\to0$ does not occur, i.e.\ as
divergence grows and every site becomes informative; Eq.~\eqref{eq:secondorder}
is therefore asymptotically exact in exactly the regime the index is used, and
degrades at low divergence. The expansion is also unnecessary on a star tree,
where the leaves are conditionally i.i.d.\ given the root.

\begin{lemma}[Exact multinomial entropy]
\label{lem:multinomial}
For $\mathbf n\sim\Mult(N,\mathbf q)$,
\begin{equation}
  \E\bigl[h(\mathbf n/N)\bigr]=\ln N-\frac1N\sum_j\sum_{m=1}^{N}
  m\ln m\binom Nm q_j^{m}(1-q_j)^{N-m}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$h(\mathbf n/N)=\ln N-\frac1N\sum_jn_j\ln n_j$ since $\sum_jn_j=N$. Take
expectations with $\Pr(n_j=m)=\binom Nm q_j^mq_j'^{N-m}$, the $m=0$ term
contributing $0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact closed form on a star tree]
\label{thm:exact}
For a star with $N$ leaves, root-to-leaf length $d$, rate distribution
$\{(r_c,w_c)\}$ and $e_c=e^{-4r_cd/3}$,
\begin{equation}
  \E[\Iss]=\frac{1}{h(\bpi)}\sum_c w_c\sum_\rho\pi_\rho
  \Bigl[\ln N-\frac1N\sum_j\sum_{m=1}^{N}m\ln m\binom Nm
  q_{\rho j}^{m}(1-q_{\rho j})^{N-m}\Bigr],
\end{equation}
where $q_{\rho\rho}=\tfrac14+\tfrac34e_c$ and $q_{\rho j}=\tfrac{1-e_c}{4}$
for $j\ne\rho$. Under rate homogeneity the outer sum degenerates to $r=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Given the root state $\rho$ and rate class $c$ the $N$ leaf states are
i.i.d.\ with law $\mathbf q_\rho=P_{\rho\cdot}(r_cd)$, which by
Lemma~\ref{lem:spectral} has the stated entries. Apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:multinomial}, average over $\rho$ and $c$, divide by $h(\bpi)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The ceiling is a function of $N$ in one convention only]
\label{cor:ceiling}
To the accuracy of Eq.~\eqref{eq:secondorder},
$\E[\Iss]\le1-\frac{K-1}{2Nh(\bpi)}$, since $\Psi\ge0$. In the saturation
limit every $\xi_\mu\to0$, so $\E[\Hbar]\to\E_{\Mult(N,\bpi)}[h]$ and
\begin{equation}
  \lim_{d\to\infty}\E[\Iss^{(A)}]=1\quad\text{for every }N,
  \qquad
  \lim_{d\to\infty}\E[\Iss^{(B)}]
  =\frac{\E_{\Mult(N,\bpi)}[h]}{h(\bpi)},
\end{equation}
the latter equal to $1-\frac{K-1}{2N\ln K}+O(N^{-2})$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
$\HFSS^{(A)}=\E_{\Mult(N,\hat{\mathbf p})}[h]$ and
$\hat{\mathbf p}\to\bpi$ by the law of large numbers, so numerator and
denominator coincide in the limit. For $(B)$, $\HFSS^{(B)}=h(\bpi)$ does not
depend on $N$ while the numerator retains the finite-sample deficit. The
expansion is the Miller--Basharin term.
\end{proof}

We prove the bound only to second order. A non-asymptotic version would
compare $\E[h]$ under the exchangeable, positively correlated site law with
the multinomial law in convex order; we do not attempt it, and the
application does not need it --- observed values of $\Iss$ exceeding $1$ are
explained by state-space mismatch rather than by the slack in the bound, since
the excursions reported in the literature ($1.49$) exceed any $O(3)$ or
$O(N^{-2})$ term by two orders of magnitude.

Numerically, the exact ceiling under $(B)$ is $0.661995$ ($N=4$), $0.840643$
($N=8$) and $0.927377$ ($N=16$). The $O(N^{-2})$ bookkeeping matters: at
$N=16$ the exact multinomial entropy at uniform composition is $1.285617$ nats
against the second-order $\ln4-3/32=1.292544$, and the normalised ceilings are
$0.927377$ against $0.932374$. The discrepancy is $O(N^{-2})$, not $O(3)$, but
at $N=4$ it is large --- exact $0.6620$, second order $0.7295$.

Corollary~\ref{cor:ceiling} is the first place the two conventions separate.
It is not confined to the limit: at $\bar p=0.599$, where
Eq.~\eqref{eq:secondorder} applies with a remainder under $10^{-3}$, the exact
star values are $0.7770$, $0.7810$ and $0.7983$ under $(A)$ for $N=4,8,16$,
against $0.5144$, $0.6566$ and $0.7403$ under $(B)$. Between $N=4$ and $N=16$
convention $(A)$ moves by $2.7\%$ of its value and convention $(B)$ by $44\%$.
Xia's normalisation is not merely a rescaling: it removes the leading
finite-sample dependence on the number of taxa, which the plug-in entropy does
not. The simulation reproduces both families to within $0.0006$.

\begin{remark}[Second-order accuracy varies strongly with $N$]
\label{rem:accuracy}
At $N=4$ --- the size used for the simulations below --- the second-order
affine line deviates from the exact expectation by $0.02$--$0.07$, i.e.\ by
$3$--$11\%$ of the attainable range of the index, and the exact chord slope
over a representative interval is $0.84$ against the predicted $1.082$. The
affine identity is qualitatively robust and quantitatively poor at small $N$;
all numerical claims about it should be made at $N\ge16$ or computed exactly.
\end{remark}

\subsubsection*{Rate heterogeneity}

\begin{lemma}[$\Gamma$ transform and monotonicity]
\label{lem:gamma-monotone}
For $r\sim\Gamma(\alpha,\text{scale}=1/\alpha)$ and $\lambda<0$,
\begin{equation}
  \E_r\bigl[e^{\lambda rt}\bigr]=\Bigl(1-\frac{\lambda t}{\alpha}\Bigr)^{-\alpha},
\end{equation}
and $\alpha\mapsto\E_r[e^{\lambda rt}]$ is strictly decreasing for every
$t>0$, with limit $e^{\lambda t}$ as $\alpha\to\infty$. Consequently
$\Psi_\alpha=3\bigl(1+\frac{8d}{3\alpha}\bigr)^{-\alpha}$ on a star under
JC69, strictly decreasing in $\alpha$, so $\E[\Iss]$ is strictly increasing
in $\alpha$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The moment generating function of $\Gamma(\alpha,\alpha)$ is
$(\alpha/(\alpha-s))^{\alpha}$ for $s<\alpha$; set $s=\lambda t<0$. Writing
$g(\alpha)=-\alpha\ln(1+u)$ with $u=-\lambda t/\alpha>0$, we get
$g'(\alpha)=-\ln(1+u)+u/(1+u)<0$ because $\ln(1+u)>u/(1+u)$ for all $u>0$;
and $-\alpha\ln(1-\lambda t/\alpha)\to\lambda t$ as $\alpha\to\infty$. Since
$\E[\Iss]$ is decreasing in $\Psi$ by Eq.~\eqref{eq:secondorder}, the last
claim follows.
\end{proof}

The homogeneous case decays as $e^{-8d/3}$, exponentially; rate heterogeneity
gives a \emph{power law} $\Psi_\alpha\sim3(3\alpha/8d)^{\alpha}$ as
$d\to\infty$. A power-law tail is heavier than any exponential, so
heterogeneity retards the approach of $\E[\Iss]$ to its ceiling at a rate set
by $\alpha$, not by any small perturbation.

\begin{proposition}[Non-identifiability of the critical value]
\label{prop:nonident}
Let $\Issc=\Iss(TL_c)$ with $TL_c$ the tree length at which
$\Pr[\hat{\mathcal T}=\mathcal T]$ falls to $0.95$. Then $\Issc$ is a strictly
monotone function of $\alpha$, and the tabulated values, computed under rate
homogeneity, correspond to $\alpha=\infty$ alone.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:gamma-monotone} the map $\alpha\mapsto\Iss(TL;\alpha)$ is
strictly increasing, with range
\[
  \bigl[\Iss(TL;0^+),\ \Iss(TL;\infty)\bigr].
\]
The level set $\{\,TL:\Iss(TL;\alpha)=\theta\,\}$ --- and hence both $TL_c$
and $\Iss(TL_c)$ --- therefore depends on $\alpha$.
\end{proof}

The dependence is not, by itself, fatal, and Section~\ref{sec:collapse} shows
that it is weaker than it sounds: over the range of $\alpha$ that matters,
$TL_c$ moves by a factor of $240$ while $\Issc$ moves by less than $0.01$. The
charge is therefore not that the threshold is unusable but that it is
mis-calibrated in a way its user cannot detect: the critical tree length does
depend strongly on $\alpha$, the index does not carry that dependence, and a
table with no $\alpha$ coordinate silently maps one onto the other.

\subsection{When the index collapses onto \texorpdfstring{$p$}{p}-distance}
\label{sec:criterion}

\begin{definition}[Scaling family]
Fix a topology with branch-length vector $\mathbf d^0$ and a rate
distribution, and scale $\mathbf d(s)=s\,\mathbf d^0$. The family is
\emph{exponentially non-degenerate} if the functions
$\{s\mapsto\xi_\mu(s)\}$, one per distinct non-zero eigenvalue, together with
the constant function, are linearly independent on the family.
\end{definition}

This holds generically. On a star under $\Gamma$-rates,
$\xi_\mu(s)=(1-2\mu s d^0/\alpha)^{-\alpha}$, and functions with distinct
$\mu$ have distinct singularities in the complex plane.

\begin{theorem}[Criterion]
\label{thm:affine}
For an exponentially non-degenerate scaling family the following are
equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\Psi$ is an affine function of $\wp$ along the family;
\item $\Delta$ is an affine function of $\Psi$ along the family;
\item there is a constant $B$ with $\tau_{[\mu]}+B\,w_{[\mu]}=0$ for every
      distinct non-zero eigenvalue $\mu$.
\end{enumerate}
When (3) holds, $\Psi=B\wp-B\bigl(1-\sum_j\pi_j^2\bigr)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$(1)\Rightarrow(3)$: suppose $\Psi=A+B\wp$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:scalars},
$\sum_\mu\tau_\mu\xi_\mu=A+B(1-\sum_j\pi_j^2)-B\sum_\mu w_\mu\xi_\mu$, i.e.\
$\sum_\mu(\tau_\mu+Bw_\mu)\xi_\mu$ is constant. Exponential non-degeneracy
forces each coefficient to vanish, and summing within a distinct eigenvalue
gives $(3)$. $(3)\Rightarrow(1)$ is the same computation read backwards.
$(2)\Leftrightarrow(3)$: $\Delta$ and $\Psi$ are affinely related iff
$w_\mu-\tau_\mu/K=c\,\tau_\mu$ for a constant $c$, which is $(3)$ with
$B=-(c+1/K)^{-1}$.
\end{proof}

The failure condition is therefore $\Delta\not\propto\Psi$, \emph{not}
$\Delta\ne0$. A nonzero composition term is harmless as long as it is
proportional to the phylogenetic one; this distinction is the difference
between a model that satisfies the criterion and one that does not, as the
F81 and HKY rows below show. To the accuracy of
Eq.~\eqref{eq:secondorder} the deviation of $\E[\Iss]$ from the $p$-distance
prediction is $-\frac{N-1}{2Nh(\bpi)}\Delta+O(3)$, so $\Delta$ measures the
size of the failure and Theorem~\ref{thm:affine} measures its shape. Both
statements are second-order; beyond it $\E[\Iss]$ depends on third and fourth
moments of the site-pattern distribution, which pairwise identity does not
determine, and Remark~\ref{rem:scope} below states what follows from that.

\begin{corollary}[Uniform composition]
\label{cor:uniform}
If $\bpi$ is uniform then $\Pi=I/K$, hence $w_\mu=\tau_\mu/K$ for every
$\mu$ and $\tau_\mu/w_\mu=K$ identically --- for \emph{every} reversible $Q$,
every topology, every branch-length vector and every rate distribution. The
proof is one line and never mentions whether the spectrum is degenerate.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Degenerate spectrum]
\label{cor:degenerate}
If $Q$ has a single distinct non-zero eigenvalue $\mu$ --- JC69, F81, and any
model whose generator is a function of a single rank-one matrix --- the
identity holds for \emph{every} composition, with
$B=-\tau_{[\mu]}/w_{[\mu]}$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
There is only one grouped pair to satisfy, so (3) is solved by any $B$.
For F81, $P(t)=e^{-t}I+(1-e^{-t})\mathbf 1\bpi^{\!\top}$, so
$P_{jj}(t)=\pi_j+(1-\pi_j)e^{-t}$, $\mu=-1$, $\tau_{[\mu]}=K-1$,
$w_{[\mu}]=\sum_j\pi_j(1-\pi_j)=1-\sum_j\pi_j^2$, and
$\wp=(1-\sum_j\pi_j^2)(1-\langle e^{-d}\rangle)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Generic failure]
\label{cor:failure}
If $\bpi$ is non-uniform \emph{and} $Q$ has at least two distinct non-zero
eigenvalues with $\tau_{[\mu]}/w_{[\mu]}$ varying across $\mu$, then $\E[\Iss]$
is a genuinely higher-dimensional function of $\bxi$ and cannot be recovered
from $\wp$.
\end{corollary}

Xia et al.~\citep{xia2003iss} calibrate under F84 with
$\kappa\in[1,10]$ and base frequencies in $[0.1,0.9]$ --- with non-uniform
composition and a non-degenerate spectrum, this is squarely inside the failure
region. Table~\ref{tab:criterion} evaluates the ratio for the models at issue.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{llccccc}
\toprule
model & $\bpi$ & $\#$ distinct $\mu$ & $\lambda_k$
      & $\tau_{[\mu]}$ & $w_{[\mu]}$ & affine? \\
\midrule
JC69            & uniform          & 1 & $-1.3333^{\times3}$ & $[3]$ & $[0.75]$ & yes \\
F81             & $(.4,.3,.2,.1)$  & 1 & $-1.4286^{\times3}$ & $[3]$ & $[0.70]$ & yes \\
HKY $\kappa{=}5$& uniform          & 2 & $-0.5714,\,-1.7143^{\times2}$ & $[1,2]$ & $[0.25,0.50]$ & yes \\
HKY $\kappa{=}5$& $(.4,.3,.2,.1)$  & 3 & $-0.6329,\,-1.6456,\,-2.1519$ & $[1,1,1]$ & $[.2833,.1500,.2667]$ & no \\
GTR             & uniform          & 3 & $-0.6224,\,-1.2568,\,-2.1209$ & $[1,1,1]$ & $[.25,.25,.25]$ & yes \\
GTR             & $(.4,.3,.2,.1)$  & 3 & $-0.5418,\,-1.1829,\,-2.1807$ & $[1,1,1]$ & $[.1228,.3260,.2512]$ & no \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{The criterion of Theorem~\ref{thm:affine} under six models. The
ratios $\tau_{[\mu]}/w_{[\mu]}$ are constant exactly in the rows marked
\emph{yes}. Two rows carry the content: GTR with three distinct eigenvalues
and uniform composition is affine, confirming
Corollary~\ref{cor:uniform} where the spectrum is fully non-degenerate; and
F81 with strongly skewed composition is affine, confirming
Corollary~\ref{cor:degenerate}.}
\label{tab:criterion}
\end{table}

\begin{lemma}[Shape of the failure]
\label{lem:delta}
$\Delta(0)=1/K-\sum_j\pi_j^2$, $\Delta(\infty)=0$, and $\Delta$ need not be
monotone.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
At $\xi_\mu\equiv1$, $\Delta=\sum_\mu(w_\mu-\tau_\mu/K)=(1-\sum_j\pi_j^2)-(K-1)/K=1/K-\sum_j\pi_j^2$;
at $\xi_\mu\to0$, $\Delta\to0$. Non-monotonicity: $\Delta$ is a signed mixture
of exponentials with distinct rates, and the coefficients
$w_\mu-\tau_\mu/K$ change sign across $\mu$.

Numerically, for HKY with $\kappa=5$ and $\bpi=(.4,.3,.2,.1)$ the ratio
$\Delta/\Psi$ sweeps from $-0.0155$ to $+0.0333$ as $d$ runs over
$[0.05,8]$, so the identity fails; for F81 with the same composition it is
constant at $w/\tau-1/K=0.70/3-0.25=-0.016667$ to all printed digits, so the
identity holds even though $\Delta\ne0$. The HKY extremum falls near
$d\approx1$, in the mid-divergence region where the critical values are
calibrated.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:affine} constrains $\Psi$ and $\wp$, and the choice of those
two scalars rather than $\E[\Iss]$ is not cosmetic. $\Psi$ and $\wp$ are exact
linear functionals of the spectral coordinates, whereas $\E[\Iss]$ is not: by
Eq.~\eqref{eq:secondorder} it carries the composition term $\Delta$ plus an
$O(3)$ remainder, and a test performed on it measures those as much as it
measures the criterion. An earlier version of this check did exactly that and
returned its \emph{largest} residual for the model whose criterion holds ---
the signature of a test aimed at the wrong quantity. Figure~\ref{fig:theorem13}
separates the two levels. Panel A evaluates $\Psi$ against $\wp$ from the
spectral decomposition alone, on a star of root-to-leaf length $d$ scanned
over $d\in[0.02,1.5]$, for models exercising all three corollaries. Where the
criterion holds, the relation is affine to machine precision: the largest
departure from the best-fit line is $1.8\times10^{-15}$ for HKY with uniform
composition and $2.2\times10^{-15}$ for F81 with $\bpi=(.4,.3,.2,.1)$, which
is double-precision residue rather than residual structure. Where it fails ---
HKY with $\kappa=5$ and the same skewed composition, the model of the last row
of Table~\ref{tab:criterion} --- the departure reaches $1.3\times10^{-2}$ in
$\Psi$ units, or $4.9\times10^{-3}$ in the units of $\Iss$ at $N=16$.
Panel B then evaluates the same three models in $\E[\Iss]$ instead, and there
the criterion-holding and criterion-failing models are indistinguishable: all
three depart from a straight line by $10$--$15\%$ of the range of $\E[\Iss]$,
and the failing model sits in the middle of that pack rather than at its edge.
The $O(3)$ channel moves the index by some twenty times what the criterion's
failure moves it. The practical consequence is that the failure cannot be
diagnosed by plotting $\Iss$ against $\bar p$, because at nucleotide skew it
is buried under the higher-order terms; the diagnostic is the ratio
$\tau_{[\mu]}/w_{[\mu]}$, which is read off the model and requires no data.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig10_theorem13.png}
\caption{Theorem~\ref{thm:affine} evaluated at the two levels it distinguishes.
(A)~$\Psi$ against the mean $p$-distance, computed exactly from the spectral
decomposition on a star ($d\in[0.02,1.5]$; dashed lines are the best fits).
The two models whose criterion holds lie on their fits to $10^{-15}$; HKY with
$\kappa=5$ and $\bpi=(.4,.3,.2,.1)$ does not. (B)~The same departures
multiplied by $(N-1)/2Nh(\bpi)$ at $N=16$, i.e.\ expressed in the units of the
index itself. The criterion-failing model is not distinguished at this level:
the $O(3)$ remainder of Eq.~\eqref{eq:secondorder} exceeds the affinity
failure by a factor of $18$ to $27$ depending on the model, which is why the
criterion must be checked on $\Psi$ rather than on $\E[\Iss]$.}
\label{fig:theorem13}
\end{figure}

\begin{remark}[Scope of the collapse]
\label{rem:scope}
The one-line argument fails exactly when the $\Pi$-average on some non-trivial
eigenspace departs from the global mean $1/K$. Three qualifications must be
stated, and the third is the strongest.
\emph{(i)}~For nucleotides the departure is small but not zero: with
non-uniform composition and a non-degenerate spectrum the deviation of $\Iss$
from the $p$-distance prediction is $0.014$ (least-squares) to $0.022$ (chord),
which is $4\%$ to $44\%$ of the separation between the symmetrical and
asymmetrical critical values, depending on the number of taxa --- the figure is
\emph{not} a single number.
\emph{(ii)}~The criterion depends on the stationary composition of the
\emph{model}; a uniform-frequency model in any alphabet satisfies it. In
practice nucleotide compositions are close to uniform while amino-acid
compositions are not, so the collapse is a nucleotide-scale result.
\emph{(iii)}~The decomposition above is \emph{second order}, and it would be
wrong to read it as a general statement that everything $\Iss$ adds beyond
$p$-distance is composition. At second order $\E[\Iss]$ depends on
$\Var(\hat p_j)$ alone, hence only on pairwise identity
$\langle P_{jj}\rangle$; beyond second order it depends on third and fourth
moments of the site-pattern distribution, which pairwise identity does \emph{not}
determine. The site patterns carry structure that the mean mismatch proportion
cannot see --- for $K=4$ a $2\!:\!2$ site is parsimony-informative while a
$3\!:\!1$ site is not, and the two have different entropies. The magnitude of
this higher-order channel is measurable and is reported in
Section~\ref{sec:simresults}; whether it is phylogenetically informative rather
than merely compositional is a separate question, answered by testing
conditional independence:
\begin{equation}
  \Pr\bigl(Y \mid \bar p,\, \Iss\bigr)\quad\text{versus}\quad
  \Pr\bigl(Y \mid \bar p\bigr),
  \qquad Y\in\{\text{parsimony-informative fraction},\ \text{recovery}\}.
  \label{eq:condindep}
\end{equation}
That test, and not the correlation between the two statistics, is what
adjudicates redundancy.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The critical value depends on sequence length}

\begin{theorem}[Length invariance and its price]
\label{thm:length}
With $\Hbar=\frac1L\sum_iH_i$ and $B=h(\hat{\mathbf p})$,
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\E[\Hbar]=\mu(s)$ exactly, for every $L$;
\item $\Var(\Hbar)=\sigma^2(s)/L$ with $\sigma^2=\Var(H_1)$;
\item $\Var(\Iss)=\Theta(L^{-1})$;
\item $\E[\Iss]=\Iss^\infty+c/L+O(L^{-2})$, with
      $\Iss^\infty=\mu/h(\bpi)$ and
      $c=\dfrac{\mu\,\Var(B)}{h(\bpi)^3}-\dfrac{\Cov(\Hbar,B)}{h(\bpi)^2}$
      after rescaling by $L$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1)--(2) Sites are i.i.d., so $\Hbar$ is an i.i.d.\ mean. (3)--(4): expand
$B^{-1}$ about $h(\bpi)$ to second order,
\[
  \E[\Hbar B^{-1}]=\frac{\mu}{\mu_B}
  -\frac{\Cov(\Hbar,B)}{\mu_B^2}
  +\frac{\mu\Var(B)}{\mu_B^3}+O(L^{-2}),
\]
and
\[
  \Var(\Iss)=\Bigl(\frac{\mu}{\mu_B}\Bigr)^2
  \Bigl[\frac{\Var(\Hbar)}{\mu^2}
  -\frac{2\Cov(\Hbar,B)}{\mu\,\mu_B}
  +\frac{\Var(B)}{\mu_B^2}\Bigr];
\]
all three terms are $\Theta(L^{-1})$ because $\hat{\mathbf p}$ is pooled over
$NL$ observations while $\Hbar$ fluctuates at $L^{-1/2}$.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:length} is the analytic content of an empirical fact the
original paper already reports. Figure~3 of \citet{xia2003iss} is titled
\emph{The critical index of substitution saturation depends on the sequence
length and the number of OTUs}, and the surrounding text uses that dependence
as advice --- a user with an asymmetrical topology and $\Iss=0.73$ at $N=8$ is
told to exceed $500$~bp if the tree is symmetrical and $3000$~bp if it is
strongly asymmetrical. Their Figure~2 likewise reports that
$\Pr[\hat{\mathcal T}=\mathcal T]$ depends on sequence length. The dependence
is therefore not overlooked, and the threshold being $L$-indexed is a
deliberate design decision rather than an error.

What Theorem~\ref{thm:length} supplies is why the dependence has the form it
does. $\Iss$ is an average over sites and cannot depend on $L$ except through
finite-sample noise; $\HFSS$ is pooled over $NL$ observations and is
$\sqrt N$ better determined than $\Hbar$; so $\Var(\Iss)=\Theta(L^{-1})$
exactly, and the critical value must move with $L$ at rate $L^{-1/2}$ to hold
a decision threshold fixed. That is the mechanism behind Figure~3, and it
fixes the functional form of the tabulated surface rather than merely
exhibiting it.

\begin{corollary}[A fixed margin does not stay fixed]
\label{cor:length}
Since $\mathrm{SE}=\Theta(L^{-1/2})$, the statistic
$T=(\Issc-\Iss)/\mathrm{SE}$ satisfies $T=\Theta(\sqrt L)$ for any
\emph{fixed} margin. A user who reads a tabulated $\Issc$ for the wrong $L$,
or who compares a margin across data sets of different length, is reading a
number whose significance changes with the site count.
\end{corollary}

Xia et al.'s own worked example makes the scale concrete: their
$\Iss=0.5573$, $\Issc=0.8093$, $\mathrm{SE}=0.01830$ on $\mathrm{DF}=731$ give
$T=13.77$, and the same margin at ten and a hundred times the length gives
$T=43.55$ and $T=137.70$. This is a property of any consistent test whose
statistic has an $L^{-1/2}$ standard error --- it is not peculiar to $\Iss$ ---
but it does mean the threshold is only meaningful jointly with the length it
was tabulated for.

The dependence is visible in published regressions without any theory at all.
\citet{duchene2022saturation} fit the entropy $t$-statistic against six
simulation variables, the variable-site count and all two-way interactions,
over roughly $3{,}100$ simulations per coefficient. Sequence length is the
only main effect with a substantial positive coefficient ($+38.7$,
$t=89.5$); every other variable enters negatively (tree length $-14.6$,
variable sites $-29.0$, stemminess $-5.7$, proportion of invariable sites
$-6.1$, imbalance $-4.1$, number of taxa $-1.1$). A statistic whose value is
driven up by more sites and down by everything else is the $T=\Theta(\sqrt L)$
of Corollary~\ref{cor:length} read off an empirical fit. It is also the
sharper form of the observation: the tabulated threshold is not merely
indexed by $L$, it is dominated by it.

\begin{remark}
Theorem~\ref{thm:length}(4) also shows the \emph{mean} carrying an $O(L^{-1})$
bias that the median does not, since the median is unaffected by the monotone
per-site structure. The median still fluctuates at $O(L^{-1/2})$, so this is
not a claim of noise-freeness; it is that the $1/L$ term, which has no
phylogenetic content, is absent from the median and present in the mean. That
makes the two a clean contrast for detecting it.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Resolution collapse in the near-saturated region}
\label{sec:collapse}

The index is bounded above, and the critical value sits close to that bound.
The two facts together do more than either alone.

\begin{corollary}[Where the critical value sits]
\label{cor:ceilinggap}
$\E[\Iss]\le\Iss^{\max}$ with
$\Iss^{\max}=\E_{\Mult(N,\bpi)}[h]/h(\bpi)$ under convention $(B)$ and
$\Iss^{\max}=1$ under $(A)$, and the bound is approached as $\Psi\to0$. The
sensitivity of the index to any parameter that acts through $\Psi$ is
\begin{equation}
  \left|\frac{d\ln\Iss}{d\ln\Psi}\right|=\frac{N-1}{2Nh(\bpi)}\cdot\frac{\Psi}{\Iss},
  \label{eq:sensitivity}
\end{equation}
which vanishes as $\Psi\to0$: the closer the critical point lies to the
ceiling, the more inert the index is to everything that produced it.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Both parts follow from Eq.~\eqref{eq:secondorder} by differentiation;
$\partial\Iss/\partial\Psi=-(N-1)/(2Nh(\bpi))$ is a constant, so the
logarithmic derivative is that constant times $\Psi/\Iss$.
\end{proof}

\begin{sloppypar}
The corollary has a quantitative consequence that is easy to overlook, and
because it carries the section it is worth setting out exactly how each
number is obtained. Take $N=4$, $L=1000$, and a quartet with $35\%$ of its
length in the internal branch. In a dedicated experiment
(Figure~\ref{fig:tlc}) the critical tree lengths at which
$\Pr[\hat{\mathcal T}=\mathcal T]$ falls to $0.95$ under maximum likelihood
are

\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{l|rrrrrrrr}
\toprule
\alpha & \infty & 32 & 8 & 4 & 2 & 1 & 0.5 & 0.25 \\
\midrule
TL_c      & 7.19 & 7.32 & 7.78 & 10.04 & 13.02 & 25.47 & 107.72 & 1716.11 \\
\Issc     & 0.9807 & 0.9788 & 0.9735 & 0.9782 & 0.9718 & 0.9692 & 0.9715 & 0.9719 \\
\bottomrule
\end{array}
\label{eq:tlc}
\end{equation}

so the tree length runs over a factor of $240$ end to end while the index
spans $0.0115$. Recovery is by IQ-TREE rather than by our own code, at $150$
replicates per point; the crossings are bracketed by the grid and located by
interpolation in $\log TL$, and the brackets are reported in the archived
output. The sweep is denser than the table shows, and the density is the
point: $\alpha=64,32,24,16,12,8$ are all run, and from $\alpha=\infty$ down to
$\alpha=8$ the critical tree length does not leave $7.1$--$7.8$, a band one
grid step wide. Rate heterogeneity has to reach $\alpha\approx4$ before the
threshold notices it at all.

The $\Issc$ row is exact, not simulated and not taken from the second-order
form. At $N=4$ the transition matrix has only $4^4$ site patterns, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:multinomial} can be evaluated by exhaustive enumeration over
the count vectors of an internal branch; those are the values of
Theorem~\ref{thm:exact}, extended from the star to a quartet by that
enumeration. The convention matters and is stated: these are convention $(A)$
values, where the ceiling is $1$. Under $(B)$ at $N=4$ the exact ceiling is
$0.6620$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:ceiling}) and the same points read
$0.64$--$0.65$; the collapse is a statement about the width of the window,
not about its location, and it appears under either convention with the span
little changed.

Because the index is so flat there, the critical points are not even ordered
by $\alpha$ --- $0.9735$ at $\alpha=8$ sits below $0.9782$ at $\alpha=4$ ---
and the small non-monotonicity is the grid and replicate noise of the
crossing, not a property of the index. That is what a quantity with nothing
left to move looks like.

There is a further breakdown at the other end, and it is worth stating
because it removes the object the tabulated threshold refers to. Below
$\alpha\approx0.2$ the recovery curve stops being monotone in tree length.
With most sites nearly invariable and a minority evolving very fast, the fast
sites saturate first and stop carrying the split, while the slow sites go on
accumulating signal; recovery therefore \emph{rises} again as the tree
lengthens. At $\alpha=0.2$ it reaches $0.81$ at $TL=308$ and $1.00$ at
$TL=2559$ without ever crossing $0.95$ downwards in the range probed; at
$\alpha=0.15$ it crosses at $TL=406$ and is back above $0.95$ by $TL=7905$.
Under the naive rule that pairs the last point above with the first point
below, $\alpha=0.15$ reports a critical tree length of $4261$ instead of
$406$ --- the two bracketing points would not even be in the right order.
There is no single tree length at which these configurations stop being
recoverable, so for them the tabulated critical value has nothing to be
compared against. This is the same collapse seen from the other side: the
threshold is a point on a curve, and at strong rate heterogeneity the curve
is not one.

The span depends on the tree shape, as
Eq.~\eqref{eq:sensitivity} implies it must, but it does not approach the
width of a tabulated row in either shape we tried.
Equation~\eqref{eq:sensitivity} evaluates to $0.005$ or less throughout. That
equation is a second-order statement (Remark~\ref{rem:accuracy}), and it is
quoted only for the scale; the conclusion it supports does not need it, since
the denominator of Eq.~\eqref{eq:sensitivity} is bounded below by
$1-\Iss^{\max}$ while the derivative $\partial\E[\Iss]/\partial\Psi$ is
bounded above by a constant, so the sensitivity to any parameter acting
through $\Psi$ vanishes at the ceiling whether or not the second-order form is
accurate there.
\end{sloppypar}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig9_tlc_alpha.png}
\caption{The critical point against rate heterogeneity.
\textbf{A}, recovery of the true quartet under maximum likelihood against
tree length, one curve per $\Gamma$ shape, $N=4$, $L=1000$, $150$ replicates
per point; the dashed line is $0.95$. \textbf{B}, the tree length at which
each curve crosses it, on axes that put $\alpha=\infty$ one doubling beyond
the largest finite shape. \textbf{C}, the exact expected index at those tree
lengths, on the same $0$--$1$ scale as the index itself. A $240$-fold change
in the first has no visible effect on the second above $\alpha=0.25$: the
threshold is nearly invariant to rate heterogeneity because the index is
nearly at its ceiling, not because it is well calibrated. At $\alpha\leq0.2$
recovery is not monotone in tree length and the crossing is not defined, which
is why the last two points of panel C leave the band.}
\label{fig:tlc}
\end{figure}

This is the resolution collapse. A $240$-fold change in the tree length
needed to make the true topology unrecoverable moves the index by less than
one percent. Across the range of rate heterogeneity where the crossing is
defined at all, the tabulated threshold therefore appears nearly invariant ---
and that appearance is an artefact of boundedness, not evidence of
calibration. The same mechanism explains why $\Iss$ is insensitive to the
divergence itself: the quantity has nowhere left to go.

Two qualifications on the scope. First, the sensitivity in
Eq.~\eqref{eq:sensitivity} is proportional to $\Psi_c/\Issc$, and $\Psi_c$
depends on the tree shape: it is small for a quartet with a long internal
branch and larger for one with a short internal branch, so the collapse is
sharpest for the configurations where saturation matters most and weakest
where the internal branch is short. Second, the argument concerns the
\emph{level} of the threshold, not its \emph{ordering}: the critical value
still moves monotonically with $\alpha$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:gamma-monotone}), just
not by enough to be usable as a coordinate. The rate-heterogeneity
mis-calibration established by Proposition~\ref{prop:nonident} stands; what
this section adds is that a user who tries to detect it by comparing tabulated
thresholds will not see it.

% =====================================================================
\subsection{Simulation: the design}
\label{sec:design}

Every claim below is checked against alignments simulated with AliSim
\citep{lytrong2022alisim} inside IQ-TREE~3.0.1 \citep{minh2020iqtree2}, under
a custom Newick topology, explicit seeds, and base frequencies and rate
categories set per arm. The one design decision worth
stating is how the tree length is chosen. Sampling $s$ uniformly wastes the
budget in the saturated plateau, where the index is pinned; sampling it from
\begin{equation}
  p_s(s)=\frac{\mu'(s)}{Z},\qquad Z=\mu(s_{\max})-\mu(s_{\min}),
  \label{eq:design}
\end{equation}
where $\mu(s)=\E[\Iss]$, makes $\Iss$ uniform on
$[\mu(s_{\min}),\mu(s_{\max})]$ exactly, since the induced density is
$p_s/\lvert\mu'\rvert=1/Z$. The normalising constant is the increment of
$\mu$ itself and $\mu'$ is analytic, so no pilot run is needed. Panel C of
Figure~\ref{fig:design} is the check: the induced density is flat at
$1/Z\approx1.56$ for all four configurations. The same panel shows why the
second-order form is not adequate for this purpose --- its induced density
drifts between $1.15$ and $1.5$ rather than staying flat.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig0_design_density.png}
\caption{The uniform-$\Iss$ sampling design of Eq.~\eqref{eq:design}.
\textbf{A}, the design curve $\mu(s)$ for four quartet configurations, exact
(solid) against the second-order form (dotted); the dotted curves are shown
past their range of validity, where they exceed the ceiling. \textbf{B}, the
resulting sampling density on $s$. \textbf{C}, the density induced on $\Iss$,
which is flat exactly when the sampler returns a uniform index; dotted is the
second-order version.}
\label{fig:design}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Simulation: location and scale}
\label{sec:locscale}

Figure~\ref{fig:lmap} maps the median and the standard deviation of $\Iss$
over a grid of total tree lengths and sequence lengths, $N=4$, $200$
replicates per cell. The two halves of the picture behave differently, and
that difference is the content of Theorem~\ref{thm:length}.

The median is a function of tree length alone. Reading across any row of
panel A, it is flat in $L$: over a hundredfold range of sequence length the
median moves by $0.5$--$2.0\%$ of its value, at every tree length tested.
This is the $L$-invariance of the location, and it is exact in expectation
rather than approximate --- Theorem~\ref{thm:length}(1) says $\E[\Hbar]$
carries no $L$ at all.

The standard deviation is a function of sequence length alone, and it is
where the $L$-dependence goes. Panel B shows the column-wise structure: SD
depends on $L$ and is nearly independent of tree length within a
$2.5$-decade range, falling as $L^{-1/2}$ --- the ratio
$\mathrm{SD}(L)\sqrt L$ is constant to within $12\%$ across the whole grid.
An intensive statistic with an $L^{-1/2}$ standard error is exactly what makes
the test statistic grow as $\sqrt L$, and this is that fact in simulation
form. Figure~\ref{fig:lmapb} reads the same grid along its axes, so the
flatness in $L$ and the $L^{-1/2}$ decline can be seen directly rather than
through a colour scale.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1_Lmap_heatmaps.png}
\caption{Location and scale of $\Iss$ over (total tree length) $\times$
(sequence length), JC69, $N=4$, $200$ replicates per cell.
\textbf{A1}, median with equal pendants; \textbf{A2}, median with pendants
graded in a fixed ratio. \textbf{B1}, standard deviation over the same grid
with equal pendants; \textbf{B2}, graded. The colour scale is separate for
each row, since the median spans the whole range while the SD does not.}
\label{fig:lmap}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1b_Lmap_profiles.png}
\caption{The same grid read along its axes. \textbf{A}, median $\Iss$ against
$L$ at five tree lengths, with the interquartile band; the curves are flat.
\textbf{B}, SD against $L$; the dashed line is $L^{-1/2}$.
\textbf{C}, the full distribution against tree length.}
\label{fig:lmapb}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Simulation: the affine relation and the role of $N$}

Figure~\ref{fig:isspdist} is the direct test of
Theorem~\ref{thm:affine} and Corollary~\ref{cor:ceiling}. Panels A and B use
the same shape at three taxon counts --- star trees at $N=4,8,16$ --- so that
$N$ is the only variable, and overlay the exact expectation of
Theorem~\ref{thm:exact} on every cloud. The agreement is to $0.0006$ at every
one of the twenty-four cells, $200$ replicates each; the closed form needs no
fitting and no correction.

Against that baseline the two conventions separate. Under convention $(A)$
the three exact curves lie almost on top of one another, and under $(B)$ they
fan apart, with $N=16$ above $N=4$ by $0.23$ at $\bar p=0.6$. The numbers are
in the caption to Figure~\ref{fig:isspdist}; the mechanism is
Corollary~\ref{cor:ceiling}. Xia's normalisation is not a cosmetic rescaling:
$\HFSS^{(A)}$ is itself a finite-sample quantity, and dividing by it removes
the leading dependence on the number of taxa that the plug-in entropy retains.

Panel C shows the main arm, a quartet with a $35\%$ internal branch at $N=4$,
where both conventions track their exact curves across four decades of tree
length. The affine relation of Theorem~\ref{thm:affine} is a property of the
process, not of the star.

\subsection{Simulation: the Felsenstein--Farris transfer}
\label{sec:transfer}

The sharpest illustration of what the index does and does not measure is a
one-parameter family that leaves the index fixed while moving the difficulty
of the problem through its entire range. Take the unrooted quartet
$((A,B),(C,D))$ with pendant lengths
\begin{equation}
  (a,b,c,d)=(p-t,\;q,\;p,\;q+t),\qquad t\in[0,\,p-q],
  \label{eq:transfer}
\end{equation}
so that at $t=0$ the two long branches are separated by the internal branch
--- the Felsenstein zone \citep{felsenstein1978cases} --- and at $t=p-q$ they
are adjacent, the Farris zone \citep{hendy1989unrooted}. The sum of the six pairwise distances is $6p+6q+4r$, independent of
$t$; and at $r=0$ the endpoint distance multisets coincide exactly, so $\Iss$
is identical at the two ends.

Figure~\ref{fig:zone} confirms both halves and shows what they cost. Along the path the
mean index varies between $0.6506$ and $0.6967$, a range of $0.046$; the
exact $O(r)$ endpoint gap at the simulated $r=0.02$ is $0.0024$. Over the same
path MPBoot goes from recovering the true topology $0$ times in $200$ to
$200$ times in $200$. The index does not track this at all: for $\Iss$
between $0.64$ and $0.70$ --- a band $4\%$ as wide as the index's own range
--- MPBoot takes the value $0$ at some points on the path and $1$ at others,
while maximum likelihood over the same band never exceeds $0.68$ and never
falls below $0.38$. The three criteria span $[0,1]$ between them across an
index interval narrower than the precision with which the index is usually
reported. This is Corollary~\ref{cor:failure} made concrete: an index
that is affine in mean $p$-distance cannot distinguish configurations that
the mean $p$-distance itself does not distinguish, and these configurations
differ by the full range of attainable outcomes.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig3_zone_transfer.png}
\caption{The transfer of Eq.~\eqref{eq:transfer}, $N=4$, $L=1000$, $200$
replicates per point, JC69. \textbf{A}, recovery of the true topology against
the transfer parameter, for three criteria. \textbf{B}, the same path in
$\Iss$ coordinates: the exact expectation is a shallow arc rising to $0.696$
at mid-path, with an exact endpoint gap of $0.0024=O(r)$ at $r=0.02$.
\textbf{C}, recovery against $\Iss$: over a band of index values $4\%$ as wide
as the index's own range, MPBoot takes both extreme values while maximum
likelihood stays between $0.38$ and $0.68$.}
\label{fig:zone}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Simulation: one parameter at a time}
\label{sec:sweeps}

Figure~\ref{fig:perturb} moves one knob at a time from a common baseline and
records $\Iss$, with no composite index and no power calculation --- the aim
is to show the shape of each dependence, not to rank tests.

Two knobs dominate. Total tree length moves the index across most of its
range, from $0.280$ to $0.929$ --- unsurprising, and the point of the index.
Rate heterogeneity is next: $\alpha=4$ gives $0.673$ against the homogeneous
$0.717$, and $\alpha=0.25$ gives $0.387$, so the transition/transversion
ratio and rate heterogeneity are comparable in effect at this scale. The
transition/transversion ratio moves the index from $0.719$ to $0.574$ over
$\kappa\in[1,20]$.

The remaining knobs are weak. The internal fraction moves it between $0.678$
and $0.723$ over a sixfold range, base composition between $0.572$ and
$0.607$ across uniform to strongly AT-rich, and sequence length between
$0.7175$ and $0.7229$ over a hundredfold range --- the last being the
$L$-invariance again, from a second and independent design.

The ordering is the result. Of the five knobs a user might vary, two move the
index substantially and three barely move it, and the three that barely move
it are precisely the ones that govern whether the topology can be recovered.

$TL=2$, $L=1000$, $200$ replicates), with no composite power index.
\textbf{A}, rate heterogeneity $\alpha$; \textbf{B},
transition/transversion ratio; \textbf{C}, internal-branch fraction;
\textbf{D}, total tree length; \textbf{E}, base composition. Error bars are

\subsection{Conditional independence}
\label{sec:simresults}

Remark~\ref{rem:scope}(iii) leaves open whether the higher-order channel ---
the part of the site-pattern distribution that the mean mismatch proportion
cannot see --- carries anything beyond composition. Reading it off a
correlation between $\Iss$ and $\bar p$ cannot answer that, because two
statistics can be strongly correlated and still not be redundant. The
question is whether $\Iss$ predicts a phylogenetic outcome \emph{after}
$\bar p$ is accounted for,
\begin{equation}
  \Pr\bigl(Y\mid\bar p,\Iss\bigr)\quad\text{versus}\quad
  \Pr\bigl(Y\mid\bar p\bigr),
\end{equation}
and it is answered by comparing the two out-of-sample.

The design must be crossed for the question to be meaningful: if tree scale
is the only knob then $\Iss$ and $\bar p$ are deterministically linked to
second order and there is nothing to condition on. We therefore vary shape
(internal-branch fraction and pendant arrangement), composition, and model
jointly, giving $720$ cells $\times$ $150$ replicates $= 108{,}000$
alignments in which $\Iss$ and $\bar p$ are not in one-to-one correspondence.

Figure~\ref{fig:condindep} shows the comparison. Three targets are reported.
The fraction of parsimony-informative sites is
exact and requires no inference. Recovery of the true quartet is measured
twice, by MPBoot and by maximum likelihood in IQ-TREE --- two programs we did
not write. All fits use a cubic spline in $\bar p$ rather than a polynomial,
for a reason worth stating: a quadratic in $\bar p$ is worse than chance in
the transition band below, and comparing against it makes $\Iss$ look
harmful over the full range when it is merely redundant there.

The full range and the transition band answer different questions, and we
report both. Over the full range $\bar p$ alone already separates almost
perfectly (AUC $0.889$ for MPBoot, $0.914$ for ML) and there is nothing left
to add: $\Delta\mathrm{AUC}=+0.001$ and $+0.002$. The
parsimony-informative fraction is different --- it is a compositional
statistic that $\bar p$ summarises poorly, and there $\Iss$ raises
cross-validated $R^2$ from $0.227$ to $0.297$.

Restrict to the band $\bar p\in[0.63,0.70]$, where the recovery probability
is neither $0$ nor $1$ and the decision is actually made, and the picture
inverts. There $\bar p$ alone is nearly useless --- AUC $0.555$ (MPBoot) and
$0.604$ (ML) --- and $\Iss$ lifts it to $0.724$ and $0.785$, gains of $+0.17$
and $+0.18$. Used on its own, with no $\bar p$ term at all, $\Iss$ reaches
AUC $0.750$ and $0.800$ in the band, and a single threshold at
$\Iss\approx0.98$ classifies $80\%$ and $83\%$ of the alignments correctly.

So the index is not information-free, and the honest statement is stronger
than "it is redundant". Two things bound what that information is.

First, the window in which it operates is a sliver at the top of the scale.
Across the band, which spans a $0.07$ range of $\bar p$ covering the whole
transition from reliable to unreliable recovery, $\Iss$ varies only between
$0.79$ and $1.03$, with the interquartile range $0.87$ to $0.97$. The index
discriminates recovery only within a few percent of its ceiling --- which is
precisely the regime Section~\ref{sec:collapse} identifies as one where it
cannot discriminate divergence. The information is real, but it is not
saturation information: the quantity that moves $\Iss$ within that window is
not the amount of substitution.

Second, part of that information is tree shape. The internal-branch fraction
--- a property of the true tree, which no user observes --- reaches AUC
$0.759$ in the band for MPBoot, better than $\Iss$'s $0.724$; and over the
full range adding it raises AUC from $0.889$ to $0.923$, after which $\Iss$
adds nothing. For ML the ordering reverses ($0.753$ against $0.785$), and in
all three targets $\Iss$ retains something after the shape is included, so
the two are not substitutes. The defensible summary is that $\Iss$ carries
genuine predictive information about recovery, that the information lives in
a narrow band at the ceiling rather than across the range, and that it
overlaps substantially with the shape of the tree that generated the data.

\subsection{Empirical: where real data sit}
\label{sec:empirical}

Everything above is about the statistic. Whether any of it bites in practice
depends on where real alignments place the index, and that is measurable. We
use the data set \citet{xia2009handbook} introduce the index with:
eight vertebrate mitochondrial COI sequences, $1512$~nt, no gaps or
ambiguity, with a reference topology shipped alongside. The alignment is
analysed whole and by codon position, which is how the index is normally
applied to a protein-coding gene.

The results are in Table~\ref{tab:empirical} and Figure~\ref{fig:empirical}.
Third codon positions carry an index of $0.715$, first and second positions
$0.137$ and $0.038$, and the whole alignment $0.270$. The source reports this
same partition, through DAMBE, as $\Iss=0.7145$: the two conventions agree to
$0.0005$ here, and the agreement is not a coincidence but a consequence of
the difference being confined to the treatment of invariable sites, which
this partition does not have.

Read against the boundary the source itself reports for it ---
$\Issc=0.7518$ for a symmetrical topology and $0.6401$ for an asymmetrical
one, both at $N=8$ and $L\approx500$ --- the partition \emph{passes} one and
\emph{fails} the other, by $0.037$ and $0.075$ respectively. The verdict is a
property of which of the two definitions of the critical tree length is
read, and both are in the table.

That is the resolution collapse of Section~\ref{sec:collapse} appearing in
real data. The partition every practitioner would identify as the saturated
one sits between the two readings of its own threshold, so that the answer to
``is this saturated?'' is decided by a convention rather than by the
alignment. The tabulated surface is also computed from $100$ replicates per
point with no interval reported, so margins of a few percent are not
distinguishable from zero.

One caveat on comparing our columns with DAMBE's, since it is the reason the
agreement above is worth checking rather than assuming. DAMBE's index divides
the mean entropy by $1-P_{\mathrm{inv}}$ when an invariant-site proportion is
supplied, so the numerator becomes the mean entropy \emph{per variable site}
while the denominator is unchanged. For the first and second codon positions
of this alignment, where $P_{\mathrm{inv}}=0.74$ was estimated and entered,
that inflates the index from $0.087$ to the $0.3335$ the source reports --- a
factor of $1/(1-P_{\mathrm{inv}})$, exactly. Both are legitimate readings of
the same construction and they answer different questions: ours asks how
saturated the alignment is, theirs how saturated its variable sites are.
Because $P_{\mathrm{inv}}$ is estimated, a threshold on their scale is
implicitly a threshold on an estimated quantity, and is not comparable across
data sets with different rates of invariance.

The informative-site counts make the point sharper. Second codon positions
hold $2$ parsimony-informative sites out of $504$ and $466$ constant sites;
maximum likelihood cannot recover the reference topology from them, and the
index calls the partition emphatically unsaturated at $0.038$. First
positions, with $4$ informative sites, do recover it. So the ordering the
index produces --- second positions safest, third positions worst --- is the
opposite of the ordering by signal, and the partition it clears most
confidently is the one carrying least.

One qualification, because a sparse partition and a saturated one are
different regimes that both end up with few informative sites. Second
positions are sparse: $466$ of $504$ sites are constant, so there is little
signal because there is little variation, and the index correctly reports
that by returning a low value. A saturated locus is the opposite kind of
case: many variable sites of which few are parsimony-informative, so the
index rises while informativeness falls. That is the association reported by
\citet{duchene2022saturation}, whose loci flagged as saturated tend to be
those with few informative sites, and it is the same association measured in
Section~\ref{sec:simresults}. Both regimes are unresolvable, the index
separates them, and only one of them is saturation. Passing the test is evidence against
saturation, as the original paper claims; on this data set it is not evidence
of resolution.

\subsection{Empirical: a genome-scale alignment}
\label{sec:jarvis}

The COI alignment is eight taxa and one gene. The opposite end of the range
is available: the largest source in the survey of
\citet{duchene2022saturation} is the avian data set of
\citet{jarvis2014whole}, whose ExaML concatenation is distributed through
GigaDB and covers $51$ taxa over $322{,}150{,}876$ aligned sites. We index
that file directly, streaming the $4.6$~GB archive rather than expanding it,
by accumulating the per-site count vector over the four states --- which is
all the index needs, and which fits in memory where the alignment does not.

The alignment is sparse: $90.1\%$ of sites carry a gap or an ambiguity code
in at least one taxon. The $9.9\%$ that do not --- $31{,}962{,}462$ sites ---
are complete columns with all $51$ taxa present, and those are what the index
is computed on. Over them $\bar p=0.0786$, $\bar H=0.1595$, and
\begin{equation}
  \Iss^{(A)}=0.119,\qquad \Iss^{(B)}=0.116 .
\end{equation}
Splitting the concatenation into $31{,}962$ windows of $1000$ complete sites
gives a distribution from $0.006$ to $0.230$, and not one window exceeds
$0.5$, let alone the tabulated boundary.

The restriction that \citet{duchene2022saturation} recommend --- computing the
entropy on parsimony-informative sites only, $37.0\%$ of the complete columns
--- raises the whole distribution without moving it into the interesting
region. Those $11{,}833$ windows give $\Iss^{(A)}=0.268$ for the subset as a
whole and a window range of $0.221$ to $0.393$; still no window reaches $0.5$.
Panels C and D of Figure~\ref{fig:jarvis} show it. The modification is doing
what it was designed to do, doubling the index by removing the constant and
near-constant sites that dilute it, and the verdict on this alignment is
unchanged either way: it is not saturated under either reading, by a wide
margin.

The value is corroborated by the theory rather than merely plausible. A JC69
star with the same mean $p$-distance and $N=51$ predicts
$\E[\Iss^{(A)}]=0.134$ exactly; the observed $0.119$ is a little below that,
which is the right sign and roughly the right size, since a real tree at a
fixed mean $p$-distance is less saturated than the star that maximises the
number of paths between leaves. Nothing about the number is anomalous; the
alignment is simply not saturated by this measure.

Read against Section~\ref{sec:empirical}, the two data sets bracket the
problem. The third codon positions of vertebrate COI sit at $0.715$, between
the two readings of their own threshold: the index is at its ceiling and the
resolution collapse of Section~\ref{sec:collapse} applies. A genome-scale avian alignment sits at
$0.119$, an order of magnitude below the boundary, where the collapse does
not apply and the index is behaving as intended. Both regimes are real, which
is why the question of where a given matrix sits has to be answered rather
than assumed --- and it is answerable, from the alignment, before any tree is
built.

One caveat governs the magnitude. Complete columns are the conserved
fraction, so $0.119$ is a lower bound on what the alignment would give if
gaps were treated as missing rather than dropped; how much lower depends on
how the gap-containing sites are handled, and we do not settle that here.
The direction of the finding does not depend on it, since the boundary is
six times the observed value and the windows span an eightfold range about
it.

\subsection{The other tree-free indices}
\label{sec:alternatives}

Two other indices are computed from an alignment alone and are therefore
available at exactly the point where $\Iss$ is used: the $C$ (convergence) value of
\citet{struck2008cfactor} and $\lambda$ of \citet{jermiin2020signal}. We
compute both on the alignments above, and the comparison turns out to be
analytic rather than merely numerical for one of them.

$\lambda$ is defined per pair as
\begin{equation}
  \lambda_{ij}=\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{obs}}(ij)}{\delta_{\mathrm{ran}}(ij)},
  \qquad
  \delta_{\mathrm{ran}}(ij)=1-\sum_k f_{ik}f_{jk},
  \label{eq:lambda}
\end{equation}
where $f_{ik}$ is the frequency of state $k$ in sequence $i$. The denominator
is a counterfactual: the divergence expected of two sequences that have
evolved independently to equilibrium. It is not a reshuffling of the observed
sites but an independent stationary process, and the endpoints are
$\lambda=0$ when the variable sites agree and $\lambda=1$ when the pair is
random with respect to itself.

The semantics decide how the quantity can be used, and they are not the
semantics of a substitution count. $\lambda=0$ does not mean no substitutions
occurred, only that the variable sites are identical; $\lambda=1$ does not
mean every site has substituted repeatedly, only that the pair has become
random. What $\lambda$ measures is how much of the \emph{historical} signal
remains --- information attributable to the order and timing of divergences
--- which is a different question from how many substitutions produced the
data. We take the framing from the source, which is explicit that $\lambda$
quantifies ``loss of historical signal'' and that $\lambda=0$ and $\lambda=1$
are definitional endpoints rather than decision thresholds; it supplies no
critical value, no standard error and no test.

$\delta_{\mathrm{ran}}$ also has a reading this paper already contains.
Setting $\xi_\mu\to0$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:scalars} gives
$\wp(\infty)=1-\sum_j\pi_j^2$, the value the mean $p$-distance approaches
under saturation for any reversible model. That is the same quantity, reached
from an independence argument on one side and from the spectral decomposition
on the other. The familiar upper bound of $3/4$ is therefore not a constant
of nature but the value of $1-\sum_kq_k^2$ at uniform composition: it is
$0.700$ at $(.40,.30,.20,.10)$, $0.590$ at $(.45,.45,.05,.05)$ and $0.932$
for amino-acid data. For the third codon positions of the COI alignment it is
$0.684$, so the rule of thumb $\bar p/0.75$ reports that partition as $32\%$
short of saturation while $\lambda$ reports three quarters of the historical
signal gone. Both follow from the same arithmetic; the constant is answering
the wrong question, by an amount that grows with compositional skew --- and in
the other direction, by $+0.18$, for protein data.

Now the part that bears on this paper. If the sequences share a composition
--- $f_{ik}=q_k$ for every $i$, the second-order regime the rest of this
paper works in --- then $\delta_{\mathrm{ran}}$ is the \emph{same} constant
for every pair, so $\lambda$ is the pairwise $p$-distance multiplied by a
constant and

\begin{proposition}[The mean $\lambda$ is the mean $p$-distance rescaled]
\label{prop:lambda}
If every sequence has composition $\mathbf q$, then
$\lambda_{ij}=p_{ij}/(1-\sum_k q_k^2)$ for every pair, and therefore
$\bar\lambda=\bar p/(1-\sum_k q_k^2)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
$\delta_{\mathrm{obs}}(ij)$ is by construction the proportion of differing
sites between $i$ and $j$, i.e.\ $p_{ij}$; $\delta_{\mathrm{ran}}(ij)$ reduces
to $1-\sum_kq_k^2$ under the stated condition. Average over pairs.
\end{proof}

This is not an approximation that happens to hold here.
Table~\ref{tab:indices} evaluates it on seven alignments spanning $\Iss$ from
$0.038$ to $0.749$, and the right-hand side reproduces the observed
$\bar\lambda$ to four decimal places on every one of them; across the seven
$\bar\lambda$ correlates with $\bar p$ at $r=0.999$ and with $\Iss$ at
$r=0.998$. As a single scalar, then, $\bar\lambda$ carries what $\bar p$
carries and inherits everything Theorem~\ref{thm:affine} establishes about it.

The scope of that is narrower than it looks, and we state it because the
opposite reading is available. It is a statement about the \emph{mean over
pairs}, and the mean is not what $\lambda$ is for. $\lambda$ is defined
pairwise, the source's own tooling plots the matrix as a heat map rather than
a summary, and the resolution among pairs is the point: no global number can
say \emph{which} sequences are the problem. Figure~\ref{fig:lambda} is a case
in point. Six taxa, one of them on a long pendant, gamma rates, $4000$ sites:
the global summaries are unremarkable --- $\Iss=0.348$, $\bar\lambda=0.370$,
neither near anything --- while the matrix separates the five pairs involving
the long-branch taxon at $0.71$--$0.72$ from the other ten at
$0.12$--$0.22$. Proposition~\ref{prop:lambda} holds exactly on these data, the
ratio being constant as it must be, and the structure that matters is
invisible to it. The index of this paper shares that blindness and more so:
being a ratio of two entropies, it has no pairwise form at all.

Two limitations belong alongside, both of which the source acknowledges in
part. $\lambda$ is built on the uncorrected $p$-distance and carries no
standard error, so near the bound its decisions are close to coin flips: at
the bound, $\Pr(\hat p\ge 1-\sum_kq_k^2)$ is near one half at every length we
tried, from $200$ sites to $20000$. The source notes that $\lambda>1$ occurs
occasionally and attributes it to finite alignment length or to sequencing and
alignment error, which is the same admission without the magnitude. And the
advantage claimed for it --- using each sequence's own composition makes
$\lambda$ ``less likely to be overestimated'' when lineages diverge under
different conditions --- has a cost that neither the source nor we had stated:
once composition varies, $\delta_{\mathrm{ran}}$ is no longer the model's
saturation bound but an empirical baseline, and the equivalence between
$\lambda<1$ and the existence of an interior maximum-likelihood estimate no
longer follows. The index of this paper does not enter that regime, since it
assumes a single stationary composition throughout.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.62\textwidth]{figures/fig8_lambda_matrix.png}
\caption{$\lambda$ on six taxa with one long pendant ($1.6$ expected
substitutions against $0.05$ elsewhere), gamma rates $\alpha=1$, $4000$ sites,
averaged over three replicates. The global summaries are unremarkable ---
$\Iss=0.348$, $\bar\lambda=0.370$ --- while the pairwise matrix isolates the
five comparisons involving the long-branch taxon. This resolution among pairs
is what $\lambda$ is for, and it is what the mean, and any single global
index, discards.}
\label{fig:lambda}
\end{figure}

The $C$ value behaves differently. It is
$\sigma(\mathrm{ti/tv})/\sigma(p)$ over all pairwise comparisons, a ratio of
two spreads rather than a ratio of two divergences, and it does not track
$\Iss$: across the same seven alignments the correlation is $-0.29$, and the
ordering it produces is not the ordering by signal. On the COI partitions it
ranks second positions ($C=55.8$, $\Iss=0.038$) as \emph{more} saturated than
first positions ($C=115.3$, $\Iss=0.137$), while third positions --- the ones
everyone agrees are saturated --- come bottom at $C=43.1$. A statistic built
from the transition/transversion ratio is measuring the substitution process,
not the amount of it, and the two come apart on conserved partitions where
there is little of either. We report $C$ because it is in use, and because it
is the one of the three that is genuinely independent of the $p$-distance; we
do not claim the criterion above applies to it.
