\section{Discussion}

The two halves of the test come apart. The index is an affine image of the mean
pairwise $p$-distance whenever the composition-weighted term in
Eq.~\eqref{eq:scalars} is proportional to the phylogenetic term --- exactly so
for uniform composition or a degenerate spectrum, approximately so for
nucleotides generally --- and it therefore reads nothing about the number of
substitutions actually realised that the uncorrected proportion of differing
sites does not already supply. Saturation, in its standard sense, \emph{is} the
gap between the observed difference and the true divergence; a quantity affine
in the former inherits the gap rather than seeing through it. The rate of loss
follows: the index resolves true divergence at the rate the uncorrected
distance does, exponentially under rate homogeneity and as a power law under
$\Gamma$-distributed rates.

The critical value, meanwhile, is tabulated without a rate-heterogeneity
coordinate, and in the region where the test is actually applied the index is
close enough to its upper bound that the threshold cannot distinguish moderate
from severe saturation. Its dependence on the sequence length, by contrast, is
deliberate and necessary: the threshold must move with $L$ because the
statistic's standard error shrinks as $L^{-1/2}$, and the original paper
reports that dependence and reasons from it. The practical consequence is
asymmetric. Passing the test is evidence against saturation --- the index
would be near its ceiling if the data were saturated. Failing it is weak
evidence, and is not by itself grounds for discarding sites; the remedy for
insufficient resolution is more data or more taxa, not fewer sites.

\subsection{What the 2003 paper got right}
\label{sec:right}

The critique above should not obscure four things.

First, the problem was real. Before 2003, saturation was assessed by plotting
transition\slash transversion ratios against distance, or by permutation and
skewness tests. Both report signal in a data set that contains two closely
related species and an arbitrary number of fully saturated ones. The paper
states that defect explicitly and attributes it to the first three of the four
approaches it reviews. The fourth is faulted on different grounds --- clumsy
beyond four taxa, parsimony-specific, undeveloped
\citep{steel1993confidence,steel1995frequency}. The 2003 paper's own point of
entry is that the fourth approach's diagnostics had not been developed
further, and that assessment has aged well.

Second, and most durably, the paper's central observation is correct: sequences
fail to recover the true tree long before $\Iss$ reaches $1$, so the quantity of
interest is a critical value, not the full-saturation limit. That observation is
what motivated later work to rebuild the test around it
\citep{duchene2022saturation}. It should also be said that the critical tree
length is defined \emph{two different ways} in the original: for the symmetrical
topology it is the tree length at which $P_{\mathrm{true}}=0.95$, whereas for the
asymmetrical topology, where the maximum recovery probability need not reach
$1$, it is the tree length at which $P_{\mathrm{true}}$ falls to $95\%$ \emph{of
its own maximum}. The two are not comparable, and every departure below is
measured on the first; the tabulated asymmetrical values therefore carry an
additional, unquantified source of drift.

Third, the simulation grid --- F84, transition/transversion ratio from 1 to 10,
base frequencies from 0.1 to 0.9, 4 to 32 taxa, two extreme topologies, 100
replicates per point --- is a serious design for its time, and the paper reports
the grid it used, together with the finding that composition and
transition/transversion ratio are negligible relative to topology, taxon number
and sequence length.

Fourth, the discussion section does not ignore rate heterogeneity. It treats the
rates-across-sites and covarion models at length, notes that the test applies to
the $(1-P)$ fraction of sites, and states that assuming $P=0$ when $P>0$ makes
the test \emph{conservative}. That claim is correct --- invariable sites depress
$\bar H$, hence $\Iss$, hence the rate of rejection --- and it is the same
channel as the $+I$ under-detection noted in Section~\ref{sec:collapse}. The
defensible criticism is narrower than "heterogeneity was overlooked": the
numerical calibration of the critical value does not carry $\alpha$ as a
coordinate, even though the surrounding text acknowledges that it should.

The failures are of a different kind: a normalisation whose entropy form
implies more than the second-order expectation delivers, a calibration whose
conditions were not stated as conditions of use, and a threshold whose
behaviour is governed by sample size and by the proximity of the index to its
own ceiling. None of these makes the reasoning wrong; together they make the
verdict the index issues unsupported.

\subsection{Relation to other approaches}
\label{sec:related}

The index has been questioned before, and the earlier objections are
different in kind from the one made here. \citet{verbruggen2007codium} and
\citet{letsch2011rrna} report cases where the tabulated threshold gives the
wrong verdict; both accept the construction and dispute the calibration.
That is a disagreement about a number, and it leaves open the possibility that
a better-calibrated threshold would work. The argument above is about the
statistic: $\E[\Iss]$ is an affine function of the mean pairwise $p$-distance
under conditions that hold for every reversible model at uniform composition
and for every composition with a degenerate spectrum, so no threshold, however
calibrated, can make it carry resolution the $p$-distance does not carry. The
two critiques agree on the practical verdict and disagree on what would fix
it.

The most substantial recent development touches the argument at an
unexpected point. \citet{duchene2022saturation} keep the entropy construction
but restrict it to parsimony-informative sites, on the grounds that constant
and slowly evolving sites distort the base-composition measurement on which
the index depends. That is the same channel Section~\ref{sec:simresults}
isolates from the other direction: of the three targets we test, the
parsimony-informative fraction is the one $\Iss$ predicts beyond the mean
$p$-distance, and their empirical finding that saturated loci are those with
few informative sites is the same association read as a diagnostic. They also
report that the tests are sensitive to sequence length and to short internal
branches, which is Theorem~\ref{thm:length} and the shape term of
Section~\ref{sec:collapse} respectively, arrived at by simulation.

What none of this changes is that the quantity being thresholded still reads
only apparent divergence. Modifying which sites enter the entropy changes the
statistic, but the modified statistic remains a function of the same
site-pattern composition, and no choice of sites makes it a function of the
number of substitutions that produced them.

Posterior branch-level tests such as \citet{manuel2025satute} are a different
construction and not subject to the criterion above. Given a tree and a model,
saturation is identifiable per branch, and estimating it there is the right
thing to do: the branch length and the number of substitutions implied by it
are both in hand. What is not identifiable is saturation \emph{before} a tree
is committed to, which is the only regime in which a tree-free index is
needed. The distinction is worth stating plainly because it delimits the
critique: we are not arguing against measuring saturation, only against
measuring it with this statistic and at that point in the workflow.

\subsection{Open question}
\label{sec:open}

Whether the rate-heterogeneity mis-calibration bites in practice depends on
where real data place the critical point on the index curve, and the two
alignments we measure answer it in opposite directions. The saturated
partition of the COI alignment
(Section~\ref{sec:empirical}) lands between the two readings of its own
threshold --- inside the collapse, where the threshold cannot discriminate. The
genome-scale avian alignment
(Section~\ref{sec:jarvis}) sits at $0.119$, an order of magnitude below the
boundary, where the index is behaving as designed and the collapse is
irrelevant.

So the collapse is neither universal nor a limiting case that real data
avoid. It is a property of where a particular matrix sits, which is
measurable from the alignment before any tree is built --- and measuring it
is cheap, since the index is cheap. Two alignments chosen for their
prominence in the literature disagree about which regime genomics is in, and
that is the argument for reporting the value rather than the verdict: a
threshold that is decisive for one matrix and inert for another is not
carrying the information its framing implies. A survey across markers rather
than two cases would establish which regime is typical, and we have not
attempted one here.

\section{Material and methods}

\subsection{Common notations and background}
\label{sec:notation}

$N$ sequences of length $L$ related by a tree $\mathcal T$; leaf states
generated by a reversible rate matrix $Q$ stationary with respect to $\bpi$,
normalised so that $-\sum_j\pi_jQ_{jj}=1$; $K$ the number of states;
$\Pi=\operatorname{diag}(\bpi)$; $S=\Pi^{1/2}Q\Pi^{-1/2}$ the symmetrised
generator with eigenvalues $0=\lambda_1>\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_K$;
$P_\mu$ the spectral projector onto the eigenspace of $\mu$;
$\tau_\mu=\tr P_\mu$ its multiplicity and $w_\mu=\tr(\Pi P_\mu)$ its
composition weight; $d$ a branch or path length and
$\langle\cdot\rangle$ an average over ordered leaf pairs and rate classes.

The two conventions for $\HFSS$ are Eq.~\eqref{eq:conventions}. Convention
$(A)$, $\E_{\Mult(N,\hat{\mathbf p})}[h]$, is the one used by Xia et al.\ and
by DAMBE; convention $(B)$, $h(\hat{\mathbf p})$, is the plug-in composition
entropy. They are related on any data set by Eq.~\eqref{eq:convention}.

\subsection{Theoretical results}

All proofs are given inline with their statements in Results. The two
numerically delicate points are worth recording here. First, the spectral
projectors must be evaluated in the orthogonal form of
Eq.~\eqref{eq:projectors}, $P_\mu=\sum_k u_ku_k^{\!\top}$, and not as the
Lagrange interpolant $\prod_{\nu\ne\mu}(S-\nu I)/(\mu-\nu)$: at $K=20$ the
latter returns $\sum_\mu\tau_\mu\approx34$ where the trace must be $19$, with
errors in $w_\mu$ of order $10^0$, because the interpolant is numerically
unstable precisely when eigenvalues are close. The orthogonal form is exact,
and we verified it against \texttt{expm} to $10^{-16}$. Second, $\tau_\mu$ is
the algebraic multiplicity as a consequence of orthonormality rather than by
a separate argument, so no care is needed in grouping eigenvalues. $K=4$ is
the last state space for which the non-zero eigenvalues have closed forms in
radicals; the criterion itself does not depend on this, only the explicit
expressions do.

\subsection{Simulation}
\label{sec:simulation-methods}

Alignments were generated with AliSim \citep{lytrong2022alisim} as
implemented in IQ-TREE~3.0.1 \citep{minh2020iqtree2}. Every cell stores its
seed, so any alignment is reproducible bit for bit; trees are supplied as
Newick so that branch lengths are controlled exactly; base frequencies and
discrete $\Gamma$ rate categories are set per arm. We use the AliSim
mean-rate $\Gamma$ discretisation \citep{yang1994discretegamma}, which is the
convention the closed forms assume: the closed form and the simulator agree
to $4\times10^{-4}$ under it and disagree at $6\times10^{-3}$ under the median
discretisation.

Two designs are used. The first is the uniform-$\Iss$ sampler of
Eq.~\eqref{eq:design}, applied per configuration with $s$ obtained by
inverting $\mu(s)=\mu_{\min}+UZ$ analytically. The second is the
Felsenstein--Farris transfer of Eq.~\eqref{eq:transfer}.

Tree shape is parameterised by the internal fraction $f_i$, the proportion of
total tree length assigned to the internal branch, with pendants either equal
or graded in a fixed ratio. Sequence lengths range over $100$ to $10{,}000$,
tree lengths over roughly $0.2$ to $100$ expected substitutions per site, and
replicates number $150$ to $200$ per cell.

The critical tree lengths of Section~\ref{sec:collapse} come from a separate
sweep: the $f_i=0.35$ quartet at $N=4$ and $L=1000$, six $\Gamma$ shapes from
$\alpha=\infty$ to $0.5$, and a geometric grid of fourteen tree lengths from
$2$ to $320$ chosen to bracket the crossing at every shape, at $150$
replicates per point. Each crossing is located by linear interpolation of
$P_{\mathrm{true}}$ in $\log TL$ between the last grid point at or above
$0.95$ and the first below it; the bracketing pairs are in the archived
output, so the interpolation can be checked or redone. The index values
reported alongside them are exact and do not come from this simulation.

Recovery of the true topology is measured by three criteria. Maximum
likelihood uses IQ-TREE with the generating model; maximum parsimony uses
MPBoot \citep{hoang2018mpboot}. Both are established, independently published
programs, and no searching criterion is computed from our own code: the search
is the part of the pipeline where an unrecognised defect would be hardest to
detect, and where a vetted program exists it is used. The third criterion is
neighbour joining, which on a four-taxon quartet reduces to evaluating a
deterministic function of the six pairwise distances --- no search, no
heuristic, and short enough to be checked by inspection. All three are used
in the transfer experiment of Section~\ref{sec:transfer}; the
conditional-independence experiment of Section~\ref{sec:simresults} uses the
two searching criteria only, since recovering a quartet from a
$p$-distance criterion is not what the index's critical value is calibrated
against. For its
JC-corrected distance we cap $p$ at $0.74$, since the correction diverges at
$p=3/4$ and returning $\infty$ would make the split sums arbitrary --- a real
limitation of distance methods in the saturated regime, reported as such.

\subsection{Empirical data}
\label{sec:empirical-methods}

The empirical alignment is \texttt{VertebrateMtCOI.FAS} as distributed with
DAMBE and used by \citet{xia2009handbook} to introduce the index: eight
vertebrate mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase~I sequences, $1512$~nt, in an RNA
alphabet, with no gaps or ambiguity codes and no length variation. It ships
with a reference topology, which we take as given rather than re-estimating.
Codon partitions are taken by position modulo three from the reading frame
supplied in the file. Sequence length is the same across codons, so no
partition truncation is needed.

The index, the mean pairwise $p$-distance and the parsimony-informative count
are computed on each partition exactly as in the simulations. Recovery uses
IQ-TREE \citep{minh2020iqtree2} under GTR$+\Gamma$, and is scored by the
Robinson--Foulds distance between the inferred topology and the reference,
over the five non-trivial splits of an eight-taxon tree (so the maximum is
ten, and zero means the tree is recovered).

\subsection{Evaluation criteria}
\label{sec:eval}

The numerical comparison reported here is $\Iss$ against mean pairwise
$p$-distance, one parameter at a time. No composite power index is
constructed and no power calculation is reported: the aim is to exhibit the
shape of each dependence, not to rank tests by a summary statistic, and a
composite index would require committing to a loss function that the
application does not supply.

Two other tree-free \emph{a~priori} indices are in use and are the natural
extension of the comparison: the $C$ value of
Struck et al.~\citep{struck2008cfactor}, defined as
$\sigma(\mathrm{ti/tv})/\sigma(p)$ over all pairwise comparisons, and
$\lambda$ of Jermiin \& Misof~\citep{jermiin2020signal}, defined pairwise by
Eq.~\eqref{eq:lambda}. Both are computed here on the same alignments as
$\Iss$, from their published definitions, and compared in
Section~\ref{sec:alternatives} and Table~\ref{tab:indices}.

For the conditional-independence test of Section~\ref{sec:simresults} we
compare out-of-sample performance of a model in $\bar p$ alone against one in
$\bar p$ and $\Iss$ jointly, with a cubic spline in $\bar p$ (16 knots) and
five-fold cross-validation. The spline is not cosmetic: a quadratic in
$\bar p$ is worse than chance in the transition region, so it understates what
$\bar p$ alone achieves and makes $\Iss$ look harmful there. For a binary
target we report cross-validated AUC; for a continuous one, cross-validated
$R^2$. Correlation between $\Iss$ and $\bar p$ is reported for context but is
not evidence either way.

Two caveats on the conditional-independence numbers. The transition band
$\bar p\in[0.63,0.70]$ and the single-threshold value $\Iss\approx0.98$ were
both chosen by inspecting the full data, not nested inside the
cross-validation, so the in-band gains are descriptive rather than unbiased
estimates of out-of-sample performance; the full-range numbers are unaffected
because they involve no such choice. And the two AUCs quoted for $\Iss$ alone
in the band are not comparable to the full-range AUC of $\bar p$: they are
fitted and evaluated on a restricted sample where recovery is genuinely in
doubt, than which nothing in the full-range fit is harder.

\section*{Data availability}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Data availability}
All simulation code, the scripts that generate every figure and table, the
per-cell parameter records and the stored seeds are archived with the paper.
Each of the $108{,}000$ alignments in the conditional-independence experiment,
and every other alignment reported here, can be regenerated bit for bit from
its stored seed and cell key. The empirical alignment and reference topology
of Section~\ref{sec:empirical} are redistributed with DAMBE and are included
unmodified in the archive, with their provenance recorded.
